source.title: Knowledge Transfer Scaling Laws for 3D Medical Imaging
source.authors: Ho-Hin Lee; Dongna Du; Chu Wang; Yuan-Kai Huo; Shixing Gu; James C. Gee; Yifan Wu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law and small-run extrapolation questions to 3D medical imaging, using MAE reconstruction loss and cross-domain data mixtures rather than language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study tests MAE loss scaling and transfer in six medical-imaging domains, and tests prediction at a held-out 200K budget. Its fixed-size model does not test parameter-count or compute-optimal parameter/token splits. Downstream scores compare pretraining mixtures, but do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. The diagonal transfer coefficients are defined as 1 rather than estimated.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of 3D-MAE reconstruction loss against training budget (volume draws) for six CT/MRI/PET domains with a fixed-size ViT. It fits on 10K–100K and predicts a held-out 200K budget. Its results therefore bear on V5 (the power-law form outside text), V2 (small-run extrapolation, over only 2×) and V7 (exponents differ by domain and data mixture). It does not vary parameters, so it does not test V1, V3 or V4. It does not test V6 either: downstream results compare two mixtures at one budget.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that domain-specific MAE power-law scaling plus an asymmetric transfer matrix lets small proxy runs choose 3D medical data mixtures. These mixtures lower MAE loss (up to 58% vs data-proportional), extrapolate to a held-out 200K budget (1.2% error) and improve downstream tasks. Their caveats: τ is held constant and validated only within 10K–200K, transfer is assumed linear, the model is fixed-size, and gains narrow at 200K (possible floor or capacity limit).
record.recipe_differences: Uses a fixed-size 3D ViT/UNETR MAE proxy and optimizes the mixture of imaging domains by volume-draw budget; it does not vary language-model parameters, text tokens, or training compute as in the cited language-model scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents and transfer coefficients vary by imaging domain and allocation strategy. The paper also reports that the optimal allocation and loss change with the minimum mixture-weight floor ϵ; its best reported floor is 5%, while at 10% Transfer-Aware underperforms Transfer-Naive. These floor-ablation results concern mixture optimization, not a test of V7's fitting-choice dependence.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-domain transfer is modelled as a source-to-target discount τij on the target's power law. The 6×6 matrix is asymmetric and has hub (ABD-CT) and island (HN-PET) structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-domain pretraining transfer in multi-domain mixtures acts as a directed, asymmetric multiplier on effective data within a shared power-law form.

record.problems: The scaling evidence uses six domains, a fixed-size proxy model, and 2–3 random seeds; scaling-result uncertainty intervals are not stated. The stated model sizes are inconsistent: Appendix C says 12M-parameter ViT, while Table 8 gives 116,679,936 ViT encoder parameters. The held-out extrapolation is from a largest fit budget of 100K to 200K, not orders of magnitude.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the six self-transfer diagonal entries because τii = 1 is defined by the method rather than estimated. Omitted downstream classification and segmentation comparisons because they compare mixture strategies rather than test downstream predictability with scale or pretraining loss. Also omitted per-domain MAE comparison values at 100K (Table 2) because the mean-loss-by-budget rows and fitted domain exponents capture the scaling results, and omitted floor-constraint ablation (Figure 5) because it tests mixture constraints, not a listed claim version.

untested.parts: All of it: there is no language-model cross-entropy and no parameter or compute scaling.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude: the tested span is 100K→200K (2×). Extrapolation in parameters or compute is also untested.
All of it: model size is fixed (Appendix A.7), so there is no parameter/token compute-optimal split.
All of it: there is a single ViT-Base-like architecture.
Scaling in parameters or compute; spans beyond about 1.3 orders of magnitude (10K–200K); natural image/video; fine-tuning scaling.
All of it: downstream results compare two mixtures at one budget (T=100K), not across scale or across loss.

missing.what: Pure-domain self-scaling exponents from the K self-domain runs: β=0.41, 0.49, 0.21, 0.24, 0.44, 0.76. This is the most direct V5 evidence.
Per-strategy fitted mean-loss exponents: TA 0.425, DP 0.325, Uniform 0.347, Naive 0.275.
Effective-budget ratio predicts loss ratio across domains, r=0.992 at 100K.

record.verdict_notes: The reported model sizes conflict: Appendix C says 12M parameters, but the stated ViT config (768 hidden, 12 layers) and Table 8 imply about 117M. Datasets are only 150–500 volumes per domain, so budgets up to 200K draws mean heavy data repetition. The 'data' axis is therefore closer to training steps on repeated data. Table 11's fit form omits the E floor used in Eq. 6. Figure 1(b)'s caption contradicts the matrix's τ direction and values. No goodness-of-fit or uncertainty is reported for the exponents; 2–3 seeds are used.

versions.untested_parts: Uses 3D medical MAE reconstruction loss, not held-out language-model cross-entropy; does not vary model parameters, language-model tokens, or compute with the other quantities non-bottlenecked.

Tests a held-out 200K volume-draw budget after fitting on 10K, 50K, and 100K, but does not test predictions for runs orders of magnitude larger. The model is fixed-size and the task is medical-imaging MAE.
Fixes model size and optimizes allocation among imaging domains; does not jointly optimize parameter count and token count against a fixed compute budget.
Uses one stated ViT/UNETR architecture and does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

Tests 3D medical-imaging MAE pretraining and cross-domain transfer across six domains. Does not test image/video settings outside this medical-imaging setup, repeated-data regimes, or scaling during fine-tuning.
Reports downstream scores for different pretraining mixtures, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable as scale changes or from pretraining loss.
Does not systematically vary parameter counting, fitting method, data, or training schedule to measure how exponents or optimal allocations change.

rows.operation_detail: Fit the scaling law on smaller budgets and predict the held-out budget
rows.measure: Average MAE loss prediction at held-out budget; per-domain prediction agreement
rows.value: Predicted average loss at 200K: 0.0227; 1.2% error; per-domain correlation r = 0.989
rows.note: The paper describes the prediction as closely matching the held-out observation. The held-out budget is twice the largest fitting budget, not orders of magnitude larger.
rows.check: The held-out budget is 2× the largest fit budget, not orders of magnitude larger. Section 4 lists 200K among the estimation budgets, which conflicts with Section 5's 'held-out' framing, so leakage into the τ fit is possible.
